handle(): wraps each operation and converts the result to response.status(200).json and errors to 400/500 (HTTP adapter work)
requiredState()/requiredText()/stateFrom(): only check the input's shape and that the state name is one of the known values; they contain no transition or business rules

No persistence, no domain calculations, no business decisions in the file
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The file belongs to the infrastructure layer, and everything it does is HTTP transport adapter work. It defines Express routes, pulls values out of the request body, query string and route parameters, and passes them to OrderService. It also turns the results into JSON responses and maps errors to HTTP status codes (DomainError gives 400, anything else gives 500). The private helpers stateFrom, requiredState and requiredText only check that the input is well-formed: a value is present, it is a string, and it is one of the known OrderState names. They do not decide what is allowed for an order, such as which state transitions are valid, cancellation rules or stock rules. All of that is left to the application service. The extra routes for /orders/:id/{paid,packed,shipped,delivered} are only routing shortcuts to the same changeState call. Two small smells are not misplaced responsibilities. First, the local STATES list repeats the names of the domain's states for input parsing. Second, the controller throws DomainError for input validation errors. Neither one puts a business rule, persistence or domain behaviour into this file.
